title: Human milk, breastfeeding and Baby Friendly
blurb: Explain why breastfeeding matters to public health, apply UNICEF UK Baby Friendly standards and support an informed feeding choice, including safe formula feeding.
question: Joy is 34 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She says she will formula feed 'because that is what my mum did' and asks whether it really makes any difference. How should the midwife respond?

teach.h: Human milk is a public health issue
teach.body: Breastfeeding protects babies against infections, diarrhoea and vomiting, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and obesity, and protects women against breast and ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, obesity and diabetes. Any amount of breast milk helps, and the longer it continues the greater the benefit. SPM 3.6 asks midwives to protect, promote and enable breastfeeding with the woman, her partner and family, while respecting her informed choice.
teach.cite: NHS: Benefits of breastfeeding (reviewed Sept 2026); SPM 3.6

teach.h: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly: the stages

steps.label: Stage 1
steps.sub: Firm foundation: policies, no promotion of formula, bottles, teats, dummies

head: Standard
In practice
rows: Recognise importance of breastfeeding and early relationships
Close relationship and feeding soon after birth
Get breastfeeding off to a good start
Informed decisions about food or fluids other than breast milk
Close and loving relationship with the baby

teach.body: NICE NG194 asks midwives to acknowledge parents' emotional, social, financial and environmental concerns about feeding and to respect their choices. Before and after birth, explain the nutritional and health benefits, that breastfeeding helps even if done for a short time, and how a partner can support. Under the Equality Act 2010 a woman may breastfeed in any public space.

The midwife asks what Joy knows and feels about feeding, then explains the benefits for her and her baby, that even a few days or weeks of breast milk helps, and how her partner can support her. Joy decides to try breastfeeding with skin-to-skin after birth. Had she chosen formula, the midwife would respect that and teach safe preparation and responsive bottle feeding, as Baby Friendly standard 4 requires.

teach.text: Baby Friendly does not mean 'breastfeeding at any cost'. Standard 4 is about informed decisions on other food or fluids. Pressuring a woman, or withholding formula advice, breaks the standards just as promoting formula does.

items: Breastfeeding lowers babies' risk of infection, D&V, SIDS and obesity, and women's risk of breast and ovarian cancer and other diseases.
Initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour, with skin-to-skin.
Baby Friendly: Stage 1 foundations, Stage 2 educated workforce, Stage 3 changes to care, then Gold.
Support informed decisions and respect choice; women may breastfeed in any public space.
Formula: first infant formula all year, water at least 70 °C, responsive feeding, no prop feeding.

summary: You can now explain the public health value of breastfeeding for baby and woman, describe the UNICEF UK Baby Friendly stages and maternity standards, and support an informed feeding decision. You can also advise on safe formula feeding when that is the family's choice.

A.q: For how long is giving breast milk alone recommended before solid foods are introduced?
A.why: NHS: breast milk only is recommended for about the first 6 months (26 weeks), then alongside solid foods.

whyNot.0: Three months is shorter than the recommended period.
whyNot.1: Six weeks is far shorter than the recommended period.
whyNot.3: Solids are introduced from around 6 months, not 12.

A.q: Breastfeeding helps reduce a baby's risk of which condition?
A.why: NHS: breastfeeding reduces the baby's risk of infections, diarrhoea and vomiting, SIDS and obesity.

whyNot.1: A mother's intention to breastfeed exclusively is a NICE CG98 1.2.1 risk factor for significant jaundice, not a protection.
whyNot.2: Tongue-tie is anatomical and not affected by feeding method.
whyNot.3: Hip dysplasia is not affected by feeding method.

A.q: According to NICE NG235, when should breastfeeding ideally be started after birth?
A.why: NG235 1.11.11: encourage initiation of breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 1 hour.

whyNot.0: Six hours is a much longer delay than NICE recommends.
whyNot.2: Routine procedures should not separate mother and baby in the first hour.
whyNot.3: Colostrum is there from birth; waiting for day 3 delays feeding.

B.q: What is the focus of Stage 1 of UNICEF UK Baby Friendly accreditation?
B.why: Stage 1 builds a firm foundation: policies and guidelines, and no promotion of breastmilk substitutes, bottles, teats or dummies.

B.q: After a full discussion of feeding, Tara decides to formula feed her baby. What should the midwife do?
options: Ask her to try breastfeeding for a week first
Respect her decision and teach safe formula feeding
Refer her to the feeding lead to reconsider
Leave formula advice until after discharge
B.why: NICE NG194 1.5.1: respect parents' choices. Baby Friendly standard 4 supports informed decisions about food or fluids other than breast milk, including safe preparation.

whyNot.0: Pressuring her is not respecting an informed choice.
whyNot.2: Referral to change her mind is pressure, not support.
whyNot.3: She needs safe preparation advice before she goes home.

B.q: Sam is asked to stop breastfeeding her 2-month-old in a café. What does NICE NG194 tell midwives to inform women about?
options: Venues may ask her to use a private room
The right applies for the first 6 weeks
She has a right to breastfeed in public
B.why: NG194 1.5.5: inform women and partners that under the Equality Act 2010 women have the right to breastfeed in any public space.

whyNot.0: She does not have to move; the Equality Act protects breastfeeding in public.
whyNot.1: The protection is not limited to 6 weeks.
whyNot.2: The protection is not limited to babies under 4 weeks.

C.q: A father is making up a formula feed for the first time. Which instruction is correct?
options: Use water of at least 70 °C, boiled within 30 minutes
Use cooled boiled water at room temperature
Put the powder in first, then add the water
Use bottled water warmed to body temperature
C.why: NHS: use water at no less than 70 °C, boiled no more than 30 minutes earlier, and put the water in the bottle before the powder.

whyNot.1: Water must be at least 70 °C to kill bacteria in the powder.
whyNot.2: Water goes in first so the measurement is accurate.
whyNot.3: Body-temperature water does not make the powder safe.

C.q: Joy, 34 weeks, says she will formula feed because her mother did and asks if it makes a difference. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Explain that breastfeeding is expected here
Give her a formula starter pack to take home
Record her choice and leave the topic there
Explore her views and explain feeding options
C.why: NICE NG194 1.5.1–1.5.2: acknowledge her concerns, explore what she knows, and give information on benefits so she can make an informed choice, which is then respected.

whyNot.0: Telling her it is expected is pressure, not informed choice.
whyNot.1: Baby Friendly units do not promote formula; and she has not yet had information.
whyNot.2: She asked a question; she deserves information before deciding.

C.q: A mother formula feeding her 5-month-old asks whether she should change to follow-on formula at 6 months. What is the best advice?
options: Follow-on formula is needed from 6 months
First infant formula suits the whole first year
Comfort formula is better once solids start
Growing-up milk should replace formula then
C.why: NICE NG194 1.5.17: first infant formula is the only formula needed in the first year unless there is a medical need.

whyNot.2: Comfort formulas are not needed without a medical reason.
whyNot.3: Growing-up milks are not needed in the first year.

reteach.title: Protect, promote, enable, respect
reteach.question: How can a midwife champion breastfeeding and still respect a woman's choice?

blocks.body: Protect: no promotion of formula, bottles, teats or dummies. Promote: explain the benefits for baby and woman, before and after birth. Enable: skin-to-skin, a first feed within an hour, skilled feeding assessment. Respect: an informed choice to formula feed gets full, safe support.

blocks.text: Respecting choice is part of Baby Friendly: Standard 4 is about informed decisions on other food or fluids.

explain.body: Babies: fewer infections and D&V, lower SIDS and obesity risk. Women: lower breast and ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, CVD, obesity and diabetes risk. Any amount helps.

test.q: Which is a health benefit of breastfeeding for the woman?
test.why: NHS: breastfeeding lowers the woman's risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, obesity and diabetes.

whyNot.0: Exclusive breastfeeding tends to delay, not hasten, fertility.
whyNot.2: Exclusive breastfeeding tends to delay periods.
whyNot.3: Labour length in a later pregnancy is not a benefit of breastfeeding.

explain.body: Stage 1 firm foundation, Stage 2 educated workforce, Stage 3 changes to care (five maternity standards), then Achieving Sustainability (Gold).

test.q: Which Baby Friendly stage is about an educated workforce?

whyNot.0: Stage 1 is the firm foundation of policies.

explain.body: Skin-to-skin and a first breastfeed ideally within 1 hour. Observe a feed in the first 24 hours, at least one effective feed before transfer home, and another within the first week.

test.q: Before a breastfeeding woman is transferred home, what should the midwife have observed?
options: A feed from an expressed bottle
test.why: NICE NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, observe at least one effective feed.

whyNot.1: NICE asks for at least one effective feed, not three.
whyNot.2: A 24-hour chart is not the NICE requirement.
whyNot.3: The assessment is of breastfeeding at the breast.

explain.body: Respect informed choices. For formula: first infant formula all year, water at least 70 °C boiled within 30 minutes, water before powder, responsive feeding, no prop feeding.

test.q: Why should a baby's bottle not be propped up for feeding?
options: It wastes formula left in the bottle
It wears out the teat more quickly
It lets the milk cool too fast
It stops the feed being responsive
test.why: NICE NG194 1.5.19: explain the dangers of prop feeding; feeds should be responsive, with the baby held close.

whyNot.0: Waste is not the concern; safety is.
whyNot.1: Teat wear is not the concern.
whyNot.2: Temperature is not the main danger.
